newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Strike to oppose P&O deal cripples Colombo port.
newsitem.headline: Strike to oppose P&O deal cripples Colombo port.

text.p: A strike by Sri Lankan labour opposing plans to lease part of the Colombo port to a consortium led by Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co disrupted work at south Asia's trans-shipment hub on Friday.
But workers began trickling back after the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA), which runs the port, cancelled their leave, a Ports and Shipping Ministry spokesman said.
"We hope work will be back to normal in the night shift," he told Reuters.

Labour unions that organised the one-day token strike to protest plans to lease the Queen Elizabeth Quay said most of their members among the port's 14,000-strong work force, which operates in shifts, had stayed away.
"The strike was 95 percent effective. The port is virtually paralysed," said Bala Tampoe, head of the Ceylon Mercantile Union (CMU).
"We're totally opposed to any deal with P&O," Tampoe told Reuters. "We're not going to allow the port to work normally unless they abandon plans to give it to a foreign operator."
The port's container and break bulk cargo terminals, usually bustling with workers, were deserted.

The ministry spokesman said only four of the port's 12 gantry cranes were working at the Jaye Container Terminal (JCT) two and JCT three, handling two container vessels while the Queen Elizabeth Quay handled two ships in the morning.
"We can work two more cranes in the evening when another ship is expected," he said. "Nearly 3,500 workers reported for work. Also today is not a day when we have many ships."
Colombo handles around 15-20 ships a day, he said, adding that no vessels were diverted because of the strike.
The strike disrupted mainly bulk cargo handling, the spokesman dded.
Labour unions have said they opposed the P&O deal over fears it would lead to retrenchment and losses to the SLPA.
The SLPA is currently holding talks with P&O to turn Queen Elizabeth Quay into a new container terminal to expand capacity and later build a new port adjacent to the present one.

The project, estimated to cost up to a billion dollars and take 10 years to build, will see the development of the southern part of the port with at least another six deep-draft berths with a capacity of two million containers per year.
Ports and Shipping Minister Mohamed Ashraff told union leaders on Thursday he would go ahead with the deal only if it was profitable.
Ashraff urged workers not to damage the port's reputation by striking, saying a deal with P&O was six months away.
The P&O deal was required to urgently expand capacity to handle rising container volumes and retain Colombo's position as a hub port, he said.
The port, with a capacity of 1.6 million containers, is expected to handle 1.3 million containers this year, up from just over a million last year, he said.
CMU's Tampoe said he feared P&O, if allowed to come in, would take away income from the SLPA's main container terminal, the JCT.
"The JCT will be starved of ships," he said.
